1: Laya is tempo — the steady interval between two maatras (also read as the 'destruction' of the first maatra's time-span when the second strikes). Three main layas: madhya (~80 bpm, roughly heart-rate), vilambit (~½ of madhya, ~40 bpm — bada khayal), drut (~2× madhya, ~160 bpm). None of these are fixed numbers — they're relative to the composition. A performance moves vilambit → madhya → drut/ati-drut (peshkaar → kayda → rela/tukda).

Layakari is the skill of controlling laya and re-distributing maatras within it for rhythmic variation — the practical, artistic side of laya. Whole-number layakaris: baraabar/thaah (1×), dugun (2 in 1), tigun (3 in 1), chaugun (4 in 1).

Kuwaad = 5/4 (5 in the span of 4 — 1.25×); Aad = 3/2 (3 in the span of 2 — 1.5×); Biaad = 7/4 (7 in 4 — 1.75×); Navamgun = 9/4 (2.25×); Ekadashgun = 11/4 (2.75×). Inverse/slower forms also exist: Poundpat = 3/4, its inverse 4/3; inverse of Aad = 2/3; inverse of Kuwaad = 4/5; inverse of Biaad = 4/7. Read fractions as multipliers: less than 1 → slower than baraabar (e.g. 2/3); more than 1 → faster (e.g. 3/2).

To write any taal's layakari: Step 1 — the fraction's numerator = beats per maatra while writing it. Step 2 — denominator minus 1 = pauses to leave after each bol. Example, kuwaad (5/4) of jhaptaal: 5 beats/maatra, 3 pauses after each bol → DhinSSSNa SSSDhiS SSDhiSS SNaSSS TinSSSNa SSSDhiS SSDhiSS SNaSSS (8 maatras). Pad the remaining 2 maatras of jhaptaal's 10-maatra avartan with pauses to land sam-to-sam, or repeat the 8-maatra block 5× to fill 4 avartans (40 maatras) without padding.

To find how many maatras any taal's layakari will take without writing it out: flip the fraction and multiply by the taal's maatra count. Kuwaad (5/4) of jhaptaal (10 maatras): inverse 4/5 × 10 = 8 maatras. Aad (3/2) of teentaal (16 maatras): inverse 2/3 × 16 = 10⅔ maatras.

Jaati is how syllables are distributed within one maatra — normally 4, but other counts are equally valid: Tisra (3), Chatushra (4), Khand (5), Mishra (7), Sankirna (9), Divyasankirna (11). Multiples are allowed too — Tisra can appear as 6 in 1, Mishra as 14 in 1.

Layakari is performed by holding the lehra's base laya constant while the tabla's laya varies — this artistic dimension may have roots in stringed-instrument practice (Ut. Shahid Parvez on sitar, Ut. Amjad Ali Khan on sarod show comparable mastery of layakari), which possibly inspired tabla players toward similar exploration. Within dashpraan, this slow→fast progression of a performance is the strotogataa form of yati.
2: पेशकार · Peshkaar

Like a plane accelerating on the runway with wheels still down — peshkaar stays close to the taal's structure while building toward takeoff. Themes (mukh) differ by gharana (e.g. Farrukhabad's 'dhinSkdadhinSdhaS' vs Delhi's TRKT-heavy phrasing); every later variation must grow out of the bols before it. Always ends on a vowel bol; 'tite' is avoided (it belongs to kayda). One theory: peshkaar evolved from theka-bhari — filling the gaps of a vilambit theka, which then matured into its own composition type.
कायदा · Kayda

Always ends on a vowel phrase. Bol choice must be mathematically arranged yet musically attractive and physically playable (e.g. 'trakeTRKT' is not valid). Expansion (paltas) may only use bols already present in the mukh — no new bols. 'Laghu kayda' phrases can fall on odd/fractional beat-points rather than whole maatras (e.g. a teentaal laghu kayda phrased 2.5+3.25+2.25).
रेला · Rela

Like a plane with rear wheels still down — close to takeoff. A rela's bol-chain may hint at the taal but its weight pattern can sit slightly off the vibhaag. Packed with rapid consonant-heavy bols (TRKT, TRKTTK), always ending on a hard consonant — the true mark of a rela. The few vowel ('dha') bols that do appear mark the rela's underlying phrase-distribution.
गत · Gat

The plane has taken off — minimal relation to the taal's structure. A fixed composition depicting natural imagery (river flow, bird flight, a bouncing ball); not expanded, ends before sum (sometimes on a weak bol, no tihai needed), usually played twice. Khula baaj gharanas composed far more gats than Delhi. Types: dupalli, tripalli, chaupalli, mishra, relagat, manjhdar, faradgat, akalgat, choudhari, sab-akaal. A thaa-dun gat is played single then double laya to show tayyari.
ठेका · Theka

Theka is taal's first bandish — the bols that outline vibhaag, taali/khaali, and overall character through an instrument. Same taal can carry different thekas depending on mood (classical/semi-classical/light) and the singer's gharana. Knowledge of which theka suits which context comes mainly from guru-taught experience and listening.
विस्तार/प्रस्तार · Variations

Peshkaar expansion is highly taal-oriented — often divided into 4 (bhari-bhari-khaali-bhari), called farsh-bandi (e.g. roopak's 7/4 split into four 1.75-maatra phrases). Kayda expansion uses only mukh bols. Rela expansion is a little freer — new bols may occasionally enter (e.g. Pt. Swapan Chaudhary adding 'dha' into tekdhinetek). Chalan/rau expansion has the most bol-flexibility of all.
गत-परन · Gat-paran

Uses pakhawaaj-rooted language (paran ≈ 'leaf' — the composition branches out from a stem). Longer than a typical gat; the bols carry pakhawaaj character (heavy, resonant phrases) extended to paran length.
उन्नत रचनाएँ · Advanced types

Uthaan — an attractive fixed opening composition (esp. Benares), fast tempo, tukda/paran-like. Chakradaar — a tihai-bearing tukda repeated 3×; simple (plain), farmaishi (each section's first 'dha' lands precisely on specific sums), kamaali ('skillful' — 27 dhas across 3×3 structure, 1st/14th/27th landing on sum). The '8-maatra method' treats teentaal as 8 maatras to simplify big chakradaar math (each calculated maatra = 2 real maatras). Nauhakka — a phrase repeated 9× with 8 equal pauses between (not just any tihai-thrice). Rou — a chalan followed by a rela built from the same syllable-structure, smoothly merging the two.
लग्गी, लड़ी, किस्म · Laggi, Ladi, Kissm

Laggi — a short, attractive drut-laya theme for taals like dadra/keherwa; variations are 'laut-palat' (back-and-forth); core accompaniment tool for bhajan/qawwali/thumri/ghazal and even Bollywood. Ladi — a 'garland'-like series with no clear start/end point, built on heavy bols like 'tite', 'ghidanage'. Kissm — theka variations that don't disturb the theka's underlying flow; some soloists (Pt. Swapan Chaudhary) open with kissm instead of peshkaar.
बोल निकास · Bol Nikaas (playing technique)

Nikaas is how a bol is physically produced for the best sound. A few core ones: Ta/Dha — Delhi strikes sharply at the chaati's centre; khula-baaj gharanas strike the chaati's inner edge for more resonance; wrist stays loose and straight, finger travel ~1–1.5 inches. Tin/Dhin — either on the sur (index finger forward, as in teentaal theka) or on the tabla's outer edge (kayda usage); naad should be more open than dha. Ge-ge/Ke-ke — full hand/wrist rests on the baya; alternating index then middle-ring finger; 'ke' uses the full hand on the dagga. Tite — index+middle near shahi's centre. TRKT — all 4 strokes equally sharp and evenly spaced; Delhi historically played it with two fingers. DRDR — whole palm, concave-up rotation on the shahi. Trake — pinky→ring→middle→index in one quick chain, paired with a 'tek'. Dhinegene — the 'ne' (ring finger, on the sur) was an Ajrada innovation enabling faster kaydas.
3: Notation lets compositions be written down, stored, and transmitted without loss over time. Two systems dominate tabla notation: Pt. Vishnu Narayan Bhatkhande's system and Pt. Vishnu Digambar Paluskar's system.

Sum = 'x' below the syllable. Taali = the taali's serial number written below the syllable (e.g. '3' for the 3rd taali — not the maatra number it falls on). Khaali = 'o' below the syllable. Vibhaag = ' | ' after every vibhaag. A single syllable in a maatra gets no extra mark; multiple syllables in one maatra get an upward curve underneath. Pause = 'S'.

Sum = '1' below the syllable. Taali = the actual maatra-number written below (so this DOES show which maatra the taali falls on, unlike Bhatkhande's). Khaali = '+'. Vibhaag-marking is only placed after the full taal is written, not after each vibhaag. Syllable-count per maatra gets its own symbol: 1 syllable = a horizontal line; 2 = two small circles; 3 = three squiggles; 4 = four upward curves; 6 = six double-squiggles; 8 = eight double-curves. Pause = 'S'.

Bhatkhande shows taali/khaali/vibhaag clearly but can't distinguish jaati within a maatra (any multi-syllable maatra just gets the same curve, whether it's 5-in-1 or 8-in-1) — faster to write, better for long compositions, and every jaati can still be expressed. Paluskar shows jaati precisely but has no symbol for 1/5 or 1/7-maatra values and doesn't mark vibhaag per-section — better for showing jaati/tigun/chaugun detail in shorter phrases, but slower to write. For exams: always include maatra-count, taali/khaali placement, and vibhaag when notating a composition.

4: भूमिका · Introduction

Sangeet Ratnaakar (13th c., by Sarangdev) names ten essential characteristics of taal — dashpraan ('praan' = breath of life — these give life to a taal). The shlok: 'kaalo maarg kriyaangaani, grahojaatihi kalaalayahaa, yatihi prastaarkashcheyti, taal-praanaa dashasmrutaahaa.' Ancient practice required all 10 in any taal; modern Hindustani retains only a few (graha, jaati, laya, prastaar, yati are the ones still significant today), while Carnatic preserves more.
१ · काल (Kaal)
The passage of time — felt across one avartan, between vibhaags, or even in the time taken to pronounce 'ka cha ta ta pa' (per Natya Shastra, which doesn't define time at a finer/micro level).
२ · मार्ग (Maarg)

The 'pathway' to a taal's conclusion — relevant mainly to ancient maargi taals, not deshi ones. Four maarg, each with fixed beat-counts and named components: Dhruva (1 beat: Dhruvaka), Chitra (2: +Sarpini), Vartika (4: +Krishna, Padmini), Dakshina (8: +Visarjita, Vikshipta, Pataka, Patita). Sarangdev himself only discusses Dhruva. In the ancient context maarg likely referred to the different ways a taal could be shown by hand while accompanying one of the seven historical geet/geetaka forms.
३ · क्रिया (Kriyaa)

Showing taal through hand gestures — still relevant today for understanding vibhaag (e.g. distinguishing ada-chautaal from deepchandi, which share a maatra-count but differ in vibhaag). Two types, each with 4 sub-types. Sashabda (with sound) — Dhruvaa (snap, hand down), Shamyaa (left palm claps right hand), Taal (right palm claps left), Sannipaat (both hands clap together) — survives today as taali. Nishabda (without sound) — Avaap, Nishkraam, Vikshepak, Praveshak (exact descriptions are debated and may not need to be reproduced in full in exams) — survives today as khaali.
४ · अंग (Ang)
The 'parts'/values of a taal, later quadrupled for deshi taals (likely to ease calculation and scale up taal sizes): Anudrut (¼→1), Drut (½→2), Laghu (1→4), Guru (2→8), Pluta (3→12), Kakapada (4→16).
५ · ग्रह (Graha)

Also called Paani ('hand'). Where the geet begins relative to the taal. Samagraha/Samapaani — taal and geet begin together. Atitgraha/Avapaani — taal begins before the geet. Anaagatgraha/Uparipaani — taal begins after the geet. (An alternate framing treats sum/visham as the two base types, with atit/anaagat as visham's sub-types.)
६ · जाति (Jaati)

Distribution of syllables within a maatra. Ancient base jaatis: Chatushra (4) and Tishra/Tryshra (3); combining them in various ratios yields Mishra, Khand, Sankirna. In Carnatic theory, jaati (varying the laghu) is the mechanism behind the 7→35→175 taal expansion (panchajaatibheda → panchgatibheda). In Hindustani practice, jaati shows up in alankaras, taans, and the composition of peshkaar/kayda/rela/chhand.
७–८ · कला / लय (Kalaa & Laya)

Kalaa — the art of presenting a span of laghus gracefully: hand position, finger spread, body movement — historically tied to pakhawaaj/mridang playing (shoulders, arms, even the left leg may move with laya). Texts describe up to 8 such movement-types (Dhruvakaa, Sarpini, Krishnaa, Padmini, Visarjitaa, Vikshiptaa, Pataakaa, Patitaa — descriptions are loosely preserved). Laya — the steady gap between two maatras/kriyaas; full detail in the Laya & Layakari chapter.
९ · यति (Yati)

Rules for how tempo is allowed to change over a performance. Samaa/Sum — constant throughout. Strotogataa — slow→fast, like rising floodwater (vilambit→madhya→drut, or partial versions). Gopuchchaa — the reverse, like a cow's tail thickening toward the end (drut→madhya→vilambit, or partial). Mridangaa yati — medium at the start, swells, tapers (madhya→vilambit→drut), modeled on a mridang's shape. Pipilikaa yati — irregular, ant-like gait (e.g. vilambit-madhya-vilambit).
१० · प्रस्तार (Prastaar)

The permutations possible within a taal's sections — also called vistaar; likely the conceptual root of paltas and upaj. E.g. 4 beats can be arranged 7 ways: 3+1, 1+3, 2+2, 2+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 1+1+1+1. Formal rules exist for writing prastaar systematically using the ang values (laghu-guru-pluta).
5: भूमिका · Why these four get a separate card

Graha, yati, kriyaa, and jaati are 4 of the 10 dashpraan (see VP-04) but are tested with enough depth and worked examples — especially jaati — that they're treated as their own revision unit here. This card goes deeper on exactly these four; VP-04 stays the one-line-per-praan overview of all ten.

Samagraha — taal and geet start at the same instant. Atitgraha (from atit, 'past') — the taal's beat has already started before the geet enters. Anaagatgraha (anaagat, 'not yet arrived') — the geet starts, and the taal's defining beat enters after. Roopak theka is a commonly cited Hindustani example of a taal that doesn't simply start from sum, which is the practical echo of this idea in modern practice.

The three (sometimes expanded to more) yati govern how tempo is allowed to shift across a piece, not just within dashpraan theory — strotogataa (slow→fast) is the shape of an entire tabla solo or vilambit-to-drut khayal performance; gopuchchaa is comparatively rare in practice but useful for understanding why some compositions are deliberately played fast-to-slow.

Beyond the historical 8 hand-gesture sub-types, kriyaa's living legacy is the taali/khaali system itself — every modern khand/vibhaag-based understanding of a taal (why jhaptaal 'feels' different from a 10-maatra taal with even vibhaag) traces back to needing to physically show the taal by hand before any instrument did it for you.

Base jaatis: Tisra (3), Chatushra (4), Khand (5), Mishra (7), Sankirna (9), Divyasankirna (11) — and their multiples (Tisra as 6-in-1, Mishra as 14-in-1, etc). In the Carnatic system, jaati is applied systematically to the laghu of each of the 7 saptasuladi taals: 7 taals × 5 jaati = 35 taals (panchajaatibheda); 35 × 5 gati-values = 175 taals (panchgatibheda). In Hindustani practice the same idea governs peshkaar/kayda/rela construction and laykari naming (tisrajati kayda is an Ajrada specialty; khand-jati layakari is kuwaad).
6: Comparing Hindustani and Carnatic taal systems shows how differently each tradition's history, intellectual style, and culture shaped rhythm. Hindustani performances draw on 15–20 main taals (teentaal, ektaal, roopak, jhaptaal, matta, deepchandi, pancham sawari for tabla solo; chautaal, dhamaar, teentaal for pakhawaj; addha, jhoomra, tevra, ada-chautaal, sooltaal for singing) with no formal 'sub-types' — thekas simply vary by context.

Carnatic has 7 base taals (saptasuladi), each defined by anudruta/druta/laghu (ang) values. The laghu is the variable: applying the 5 jaati (chatushra 4, tryshra 3, khand 5, mishra 7, sankirna 9) to each of the 7 base taals gives 7×5 = 35 taals (panchajaatibheda) — e.g. Dhruva taal's khand form: laghu(5)+druta(2)+laghu(5)+laghu(5) = 17 maatras. Applying the 5 gati values to each of those 35 gives 35×5 = 175 taals (panchgatibheda).

Main instruments: Hindustani — tabla, pakhawaaj; Carnatic — mridangam, ghatam. Accompanist's freedom: limited in Hindustani; mridangam/ghatam players get notably more solo space within a Carnatic performance. Taal composition logic: Hindustani builds on maatra+vibhaag (no jaati/gati-bhed framework); Carnatic builds on laghu and its permutations. Start point: Carnatic taals always start from sum; Hindustani has exceptions (roopak). Khaali: present in Hindustani, absent in Carnatic (which uses ang-distribution instead). Laya range: Hindustani explores the full range; Carnatic rarely uses ativilambit or anudrut layas.

Broadly: in Hindustani music the taal's basics stay fixed and composition/vistaar happens within that frame; in Carnatic music the mathematics begins inside the taal itself, expanded systematically to its fullest extent.
7: Sage Bharat Muni's Natya Shastra classifies all instruments into 4 groups. Tat Vadya (stringed, plucked/struck — Veena, Sitar, Sarod, Santoor). Vitat Vadya (stringed, bowed — friction of bow on string — Sarangi, Violin, Dilruba, Tar-Shehnai). Sushir Vadya (wind, blown — Shehnai, Clarinet, Harmonium, where bellows-driven air vibrates a reed). Avanaddha Vadya (percussion/membranophone — wood/mud/metal/stone body with an animal-hide face). Ghana Vadya (idiophone — metal-on-metal, e.g. Tal, Ghunghroo, Jhanjh; Tal is common in bhajans).

Ancient Bhoomi-Dundubhi (a hide stretched over a dug pit, struck with sticks) is among the earliest percussion concepts. Per legend, Sage Swati noticed water trickling over lotus leaves and was inspired to create instruments like Mridang, Dundhubi, Aalingya, Urdhwak, and Ankik. Old textual instruments: Tripushkar, Mridang, Damru. Modern-day instruments: Pakhawaaj, Tabla, Dholki, Dholak, Dhol, Daf. Stringed and wind instruments can produce multiple swar; idiophones and avanaddha instruments like tabla are tuned to one note only, but both idiophones and avanaddha instruments help anchor laya/taal for the main artist.
भारतीय बनाम पश्चिमी पर्क्शन · Indian vs Western percussion

Western percussion is grouped as idiophones (xylophone, cymbals, gong — full-body vibration) and membranophones (drums — snare, bass, tenor). Because idiophones map to ghana vadya in the Indian system, the meaningful comparison is avanaddha vadya vs Western membranophones. Bass drum — large, two-headed, deep low boom, played with felt-headed sticks. Snare drum — small cylindrical drum, struck with two round-tipped sticks, originally military. Djembe (African origin) is hand-played, closer in spirit to Indian technique.

Playing method — Indian instruments mostly hand-played; Western mostly stick-played (rounded tips, varying size/material). Shahi — Indian instruments have a tuned shahi portion on the face; Western drums don't. Dr. C.V. Raman found shahi gives ~20% more resonance and longer aas — Western drums lack this but compensate with stick-speed (staccato, fast rolls not possible on Indian avanaddha instruments). Solo role — more central in Indian performance; present but secondary to ensemble role in the West. Laya rules — Western percussion needn't follow the slow→fast progression tabla performances do; per Pt. Suresh Talwalkar, Western instruments (lacking aas) can't really carry a peshkaar-style vilambit presentation.
संगति-वाद्य (विशेष नाम) · Named accompaniment percussion (avanaddha family)

Pakhawaaj — tabla's likely 'father' instrument; horizontal double-faced barrel drum; dhrupad's primary percussion accompaniment; Punjab gharana's open bols (GDNG, dhagetete tagetete) trace to pakhawaaj influence. Mridangam — Carnatic counterpart, smaller than pakhawaaj, left face finger-played (not palm); jackfruit-wood body, sheepskin faces; bols include chapu, dhi, tha, tom. Dholak — horizontal hand-drum (qawwali/lavani/kirtan/bhangra); larger buffalo-skin face with shahi (lower pitch), smaller goatskin face (sharper). Dholki/Naal — smaller, goat skin both sides on an iron ring, very high-pitched, central to Maharashtrian tamasha/lavani and Hindi film songs. Khol — asymmetric horizontal drum, fixed pitch, popular in Bengali/Rabindra Sangeet and ISKCON kirtan. Sambal — two attached drums (wood+brass), played standing with bent-tip sticks; Maharashtra processions, Ganpati visarjan. Gudum Baja — Gond-tribe (Madhya Pradesh) drum-set, played standing, struck with curved sticks/elbows. Tavil — South Indian barrel drum accompanying the nadaswaram; jackfruit-wood body, water-buffalo skin one side/goatskin other; struck with stick on one side, finger-caps on the other.
तार व सुषिर संगति-वाद्य · Named string/wind accompaniment

Tanpura — long-necked drone instrument (4-string cycle), sized to the singer's pitch; sets the harmonic base for raga. Harmonium — bellows-pumped reed box; designed by Kratzenstein (Copenhagen, 1700s), hand-pumped version by Dwarkanath Ghose (Calcutta, 1875); strong sustained notes suit vocal accompaniment. Shehnai — double-reed wind instrument, 7 finger-holes, associated with royal/auspicious occasions and weddings; Ustad Bismillah Khan is credited with bringing it into the classical concert space. Ektara — one-stringed folk instrument family (gopichand, tuntuna, tumbi variants across regions).
10: Sangeet Makarand — the practical, cyclical division of time in music. Sangeet Ratnakar — the medium through which vocal music, instrumental music, and dance establish themselves. Sage Bharat Muni — the medium measuring the activities of vocal/instrumental music and dance. Sangeet Chintamani — the counting/striking by hand, or opening/closing fingers, during a performance. Common thread: taal is fundamentally a tool of measurement, built on a pre-conceived, stable, cyclically-flowing idea of time, graspable through both sashabda (with sound) and nishabda (without sound) means.
ताल बनाने की प्रक्रिया · Creation process

Step 1 — fix the maatra-count (dhrupad/dhamaar use large counts; khayal taals are usually ≤16; shorter taals suit shringar rasa, longer ones suit shanta rasa). Step 2 — divide into khand/vibhaag. Step 3 — fix taali/khaali placement. Step 4 — fill with bols appropriate to the taal's character. (Full design rules, including khand min/max size and khaali-repetition restrictions, are covered in the next card, VP-19.)

Theka is the use of organised bols on an instrument to express a particular taal — taal's 'first bandish.' A taal alone doesn't give you a theka; multiple thekas can exist for one taal (tilwada and punjabi theka share teentaal's vibhaag but differ in bol-treatment), and the changes within a theka can never distort the taal's own boundaries. Dhrupad/dhamaar favour khula (open) bols in theka; khayal's vilambit theka may decorate the gap between maatras with extra bols to fill the resonance-gap before khaali or sum.

ताल-तुलना का ढाँचा · Comparison framework (for writing answers)

When asked to compare two taals with the same maatra-count, structure the answer around: maatra-count, vibhaag pattern, taali/khaali placement, theka, and typical use (which gayan/vadan style). Two taals sharing a maatra-count is common (e.g. 14-maatra taals) — the vibhaag split and use-context are what actually distinguish them, which is the point most often tested.
19: Decide total maatras first. In accompaniment this often follows the main artist's composition type — dhrupad/dhamaar use large maatra-counts; khayal-suited taals stay shorter (≤16). Rasa connects to length: shringar rasa (love/attraction/light theme) suits shorter taals — ghazal uses dadra (6), roopak (7), keherwa (8); shanta/gambhir rasa (serious, detail-heavy) suits longer taals played vilambit/madhya, giving more canvas.

⚑ Source note: Eshan's raw file states each vibhaag may have a minimum of 2 and maximum of 5 maatras. This card's settled skeleton states minimum 3 — which, per project rule, is the answer to use in the exam since settled-card content already reflects paper cross-verification done in the original VP-19 build. New taals generally try a different khand/vibhaag pattern than any existing taal of the same maatra-count, so the new taal has its own identity rather than being 'just another theka' of something that already exists.
Khaali placement should feel meaningful, not arbitrary, and no element of the taal should be dragged on too long. Khaali is never repeated twice in a row.

Bols should suit the taal's intended character. Bols like 'din' or 'titekatagadigena' signal khula-baaj/pakhawaaj-rooted taals and won't sit well if forced into a band-baaj treatment; conversely most other taals can be played in either baaj as required.
13: भूमिका · The 6 gharanas at a glance

Band baaj — Delhi, Ajrada. Khula baaj — Lucknow (poorab baaj), Farrukhabad, Benares, Punjab. Delhi accepted band baaj directly; Lucknow accepted khula baaj (also called poorab baaj). Ajrada is a disciple-gharana of Delhi; Farrukhabad and Benares are disciple-gharanas of Lucknow; Punjab is independent of Delhi and also took khula baaj.

Founder: Ut. Siddhar Khan Dhadi. Band baaj — 'do-oongli ka baaj'/'chaati ka baaj' (mainly index+middle finger). Considered the aadya (first) gharana; the most restrictive/rule-bound. Strong on peshkaar/kayda/rela (expansion-heavy), weak on gat/tukda (which need open-hand/palm playing). Even peshkaar is expanded kayda-style — strictly bol-sequence-bound. Mostly chatushra-jati kaydas, mukhda-mala with odd weightage; speed is naturally limited by the two-finger technique, so Delhi compensates with depth of expansion. Key figures: Ut. Gamey Khan (introduced taals beyond teentaal), Ut. Inam Ali Khan (last major khalifa to keep the baaj 'pure'; introduced a khaali-starting roopak peshkaar).

Founders: Miru Khan and Kallu Khan (originally Delhi students). Band baaj — added the ring finger to Delhi's two-finger base, enabling more speed and new bols like dhinegene. Specialised in tisra-jati kaydas (a genuine point of difference from Delhi's chatushra focus), with strong baya use (gheeskaam, meend) for sweetness, used sparingly. Khaali is sometimes blended into the kayda itself rather than kept cleanly separate. Key figure: Ut. Habibuddin Khan (learned gat-tode elements from Farrukhabad's Ut. Munir Khan and folded them back into Ajrada kaydas).

Founders: Ut. Modu Khan and Ut. Bakshu Khan (Delhi-trained, but reshaped for Lucknow's kathak culture). Khula baaj — also 'hatheli ka baaj'/'thapeeya ka baaj.' Plays many more tukdas and gats than kaydas (and what kaydas exist carry gat-like language); paran was adapted from pakhawaaj, with smaller extracted pieces eventually becoming today's tukdas. Plays on luv (tabla) and maidan (baya) rather than chaati for a more 'open' sound — sweeter but slower (less suited to fast kayda work). Key figure: Ut. Wajid Hussain Khan (gat/gat-paran/rela specialist known for a distinctive 'rav').

Founder: Ut. Haji Vilayat Ali Khan (went on Haj seven times, hence 'Haji'). Khula baaj, very close in feel to Lucknow but with its own signature phrase 'DRDRKTTK takite dha' stamped across many gats/gat-tukdas. Strong across peshkaar/kayda/rela AND gat/gat-paran/gat-tode — a comprehensive gharana. Kayda sequence convention: mukh, laut-palat, tihai (vs. Delhi's mukh-dohra-bala-palta-tihai). Mostly chatushra jati, occasional tisra; teentaal kaydas can run up to 32 maatras. Key figures: Ut. Munir Khan (his student, taught 24 gurus' worth of styles — see VP-15), Ut. Amir Hussain Khan, Ut. Ahmedjaan Thirakwa.

Founder: Pt. Ram Sahai Mishra (not blood-linked to Delhi; devout Hindu lineage, instruments treated as sacred). Khula baaj — opens with uthaan (often 'tin darje ki uthaan', single then tisra jati), not peshkaar; plays more on luv; baya's maidan faces the audience (opposite of most gharanas), aiding gheeskaam/meend expression. Players historically sat in vajrasan for a 'punch'-heavy attack. Specialises in fard/ekkad — abrupt, joda-resistant compositions that land on sum without warning. Famous single-finger 'na din din na' ('khadi oongli ka'). Uses high-pitched 'tip tabla'. Key figures: Pt. Kanthe Maharaj, Pt. Kishan Maharaj, Pt. Samta Prasad, Pt. Anokhelal Mishra.

Founder: Lala Bhawanidas Pakhawaaji (a pakhawaaj player by background — see VP-17's origin legend). Khula baaj, heavy pakhawaaj influence (loud, open-bol character). Originally lacked kayda/peshkaar — Ut. Alla Rakha later composed his own for the gharana. Distinctive odd-number phrase splits (e.g. 7,9,7,9 instead of typical teentaal divisions) and unusual dum-lengths (1¼, 1¾ maatra pauses) in tihais, plus Punjabi-language-influenced pronunciation (e.g. 'dha na' → 'dha णा'). Deepchandi-weighted chaal and mishra-jati gats are a specialty. Key figures: Ut. Alla Rakha, Ut. Zakir Hussain.

GHARANA_ATTRIBUTES.docx adds finer style-comparison detail on top of the above — Delhi-vs-Farrukhabad peshkaar contrast, Delhi-vs-Ajrada baya/gheeskaam contrast, and extra Benares performance detail. Worth a look if a paper asks specifically for a head-to-head between two named gharanas rather than a standalone description.
16: घराना का अर्थ · Meaning of Gharana

A musical lineage/tradition. Historically, students memorised under a guru for at least 12 years before performing publicly. Out of many students learning the same way, occasionally one would absorb other styles and create something distinct — if that new style held for at least 3 generations, a new gharana was considered formed (usually named after that player's hometown).
गठन के कारण · Why new gharanas formed

Two real distinguishing factors separate gharanas: baaj (playing style) and — more significantly — thought-system (vichaardhara). Delhi and Ajrada share the same baaj (band baaj) but differ in thought-system and nikaas, which is why they're still considered separate gharanas. New gharanas could also emerge from a student's dissatisfaction/curiosity, or from regional/geopolitical circumstance providing a different stimulus for thinking.
बाज का अर्थ · Meaning of Baaj
Baaj (from Hindi 'bajana') is playing style — the two umbrella types are band baaj and khula baaj.

Bols are played prominently on the chaati (tabla) and luv (baya); the hand generally isn't lifted while playing. Limited resonance means a second bol must follow quickly to sustain energy — this is exactly why band-baaj gharanas (Delhi, Ajrada) developed so many kaydas. No pakhawaaj-style palm/maidan sound here.

The opposite of band baaj — luv/sur playing dominates, with clear pakhawaaj influence (more resonance, 'open' sound). Speed matters less here than in band baaj; gat, gat-paran, and chakradaar are prominent. Gharanas: Lucknow (poorab baaj), Farrukhabad, Benares, Punjab.

Many practitioners hold that there's effectively 'one baaj' in active practice now — players intermix material from different gharanas freely, requiring baaj-flexibility, and the historically separate teachings have diversified and merged through cross-learning.
14: Surviving/documented gharanas: Nana Panse, Nathdwara (Mewad), Kudau Singh, Jawali, Koriya (Mathura), Punjab, Mangalwedhekar, and some lesser-known families from Bengal.

Founder Nanasaheb Panse (Bavdhan, near Wai, Maharashtra) — trained under his father, then under Shri Kotadikar at Pune, then 12 years at Kashi before settling in Indore. Simplified and systematised pakhawaj teaching using maatra-bound, mathematically-justified method; created new thekas/paran. Highlights: simpler/clearer technique, smaller paran, melodious fast relas, bols like Dhum Kit/GaDiGaNe/TakTak, 'laybandh' (compositions first set in laya/taal, then performed), a signature 3-3 maatra khand calculation. Generally seen as softer/more poetic than Kudau Singh's more forceful style.

Founder Pt. Tulsiram ji, ~250-300 years old, rooted in devotional (temple-funded) musicianship near Jaipur. Pandit Rupram ji (5th generation) gave the gharana its lasting identity, serving Shri Nath Ji at Nathdwara. Style close to Kudau Singh's; uses 'Kit' where others might use 'Tit' (common phrases: dhaKitTek, TaKiTeTak, TRKTTak, KTTK, KidheTiTe).

Kudau Singh ji — disciple of Bhavanidas, royal artist at Datia Darbar (b. 1812 Banda village UP, d. 1907); devotee of Goddess Kali; received the title 'Singh' after Bhavanidas's death. Specialises in complex, lengthy, joyful-yet-solemn paran (5 to 24 avartans long), with clear nikaas and hand dexterity. Common bols: Ghadann, Dhadann, Tadanna, DhumakiTe, Dhetta, Takka, Thunga. ⚑ Lineage note: Kudau Singh's guru-chain (via Koriya gharana → Bhavanidas → Kudau Singh) is the item flagged amber pending guru confirmation in the wider project — treat the exact generational chain with caution until settled.

Jawali — considered the oldest pakhawaj gharana (the 'Delhi' of pakhawaj), founded by Pandit Bhagwandas after Akbar gifted him the town of Jawali; little performance-style detail survives. Koriya (Mathura) — traced to a disciple of Swami Vallabhacharya cured of leprosy (kod/kusthrog → 'Kodhiya' → Koriya); Bhavanidas himself descends from this line. Punjab — linked to Bhavanidas through disciple Taj Khan and his son Nasir Khan; sub-lines include Kanta Prasad/Nasir Hussain and Hussain Baksh/Fakir Baksh. Mangalwedhekar — founded by Pandit Vitthalacharya (a temple Gurav at Mangalwedha), shaped for bhajan/kirtan accompaniment; known for a powerful 'jorkas' style, strong laybaat (layakari), and full-palm bol technique.
15: UT__MUNIR_KHAN_BIOGRAPHY.docx is word-for-word the same text as the Munir Khan entry already inside BIOGRAPHIES_TABLA_AND_PAKHAWAAJ_PLAYERS.docx — it is not additional/extended material, just a duplicate standalone copy. The handoff's hypothesis that 'both files are likely needed' doesn't hold once actually compared; only one copy of the text is used below.

Ut. Ahmedjaan Thirakwa (1881–1976, Muradabad) — learned under Ut. Munir Khan for 26 years; 14–15 hrs/day riyaaz; popularised peshkaar 'dhinSkda dhina Sdha dhina'; Sangeet Natak Akademi, Padmabhushan (1970). Ut. Amir Hussain Khan (1899–1969, Bankhanda) — Munir Khan's nephew; renowned 2-finger DRDR; played 4 hrs for the Maharaj of Raigad for 1,000 gold coins; left-handed (baya with right hand). Ut. Munir Khan (1863–1936, Laliyana) — see VP-13/VP-16 for his Bumbai-gharana synthesis of all 6 gharanas; taught 24 gurus' worth of material to disciples including Thirakwa, Amir Hussain Khan, Habibuddin Khan. Ut. Keramatullah Khan (1918–1977, Rampur) — son/student of Ut. Masit Khan; Farrukhabad baaj with strong Benares influence; noted for string-instrument accompaniment. Ut. Salaari Khan — senior disciple of Haji Vilayat Ali Khan alongside Imam Baksh; known for composing 'jod' (responses) to Haji saab's compositions. Ut. Chudiyawale Imam Baksh — originally a pakhawaaj player; served Haji Vilayat Ali Khan as hukkah-assistant before being accepted as disciple; received a bangle (chudiya) instead of a thread at his ganda-bandhan, hence the name.

Ut. Gamey Khan — learned from father Ut. Chhote Kale Khan (age 5–15); Delhi khalifa; father of Ut. Inam Ali Khan. Ut. Inam Ali Khan (1928–1988, Delhi) — son of Gamey Khan; among the last to preserve authentic 2-finger/do-oongli Delhi baaj; introduced a khaali-starting roopak peshkaar. Ut. Natthu Khan (1875–1940, Delhi) — son of Ut. Bolibaksh Khan; 16–18 hrs/day riyaaz; fast 2-finger DRDR kaydas; taught Ut. Habibuddin Khan.

Ut. Habibuddin Khan (1899–1972, Meerut) — trained under father Shammu Khan, then Delhi's Natthu Khan, then Munir Khan; vast compositional memory (famously challenged audiences to catch him repeating a piece on consecutive days); Sangeet Natak Akademi. Ut. Shammu Khan (1876–1935, Meerut) — father/teacher of Habibuddin Khan.

Ut. Wajid Hussain (1906–, Lucknow) — son of Ut. Bade Munne Khan; learned from father and Ut. Abid Hussain Khan; known for a distinctive 'rav' in gat/gat-paran/rela. Ut. Abid Hussain (1867–1936, Lucknow) — son of Ut. Mohammad Khan; taught at Marris Music College (now Bhatkhande Hindustani Sangeet Mahavidyalaya), Lucknow.

Ut. Alla Rakha (1915–2000, Gurdaspur) — trained under Ut. Kaadir Baksh at Lahore; accompanied Pt. Ravi Shankar, Pt. Birju Maharaj, Ut. Ali Akbar Khan; also a Hindi-film music director; introduced the ¼-maatra-dum tihai; Padma Shri (1977); father of Ut. Zakir Hussain. Pt. Samta Prasad / Gudai Maharaj (1920–1994, Varanasi) — trained under father Pt. Baachaa Mishra, then Pt. Vikramaditya Mishra; tabla in films (Jhanak Jhanak Payal Baje, Basant Bahar, Sholay); Padma Shree (1972), Padma Bhushan; specialist in DRDR/TRKT/taktak and in roopak/dhamaar. Pt. Kanthe Maharaj (b. ~1880, Benares) — trained under Pt. Baldev Sahai; contributed extensively to Benares gats/paran/chhand; uncle/guru of Pt. Kishan Maharaj.

Pt. Purshottam Das Pakhwaji (1907–1991, Mewad) — son of Mridang Sagar author Shri Ghanashyam Pakhwaji; raised/trained by Shri Govardhanlalji Maharaj after his father's early death; Padma Shri. Pt. Madhavrao Algutkar — Nana Panse-gharana representative; accompanied Ut. Amir Hussain Khan. Pt. Sakharamji Gurav — Indore-based, trained under Shri Shankar Panse; later professor at Marris Music College, Lucknow; authored Mrudung Tabla Shiksha. Pt. Govindrao Barhanpurkar (d. 1957) — trained under a Nana Panse disciple, then Dhrupad-Dhamar under Harihar Bua, then tabla under Pt. Vamanrao; toured with Pt. Vishnu Digambar Paluskar; published Mrudang aur Tabla Vadan Subodh and Bharatiya Taal Manjiri; Mrudangacharya (1929). Pt. Parvat Singh (1879–1951, Gwalior) — Gwalior court pakhawaj player, succeeding a family line (grandfather Jorawar Singh, father Sukhdev Singh). Pt. Ayodhya Prasad (1891–1977, Datia) — son of Pandit Gaya Prasad; learned mrudang under Shri Ram Singh and his father; favoured chaartaal; Padma Shri. Swami Paagaldasji/Shri Ramshankar Das (1920–1997) — preserved the Kudau Singh pakhawaj tradition; founded Hanumat Vishwakala Sangeetashram. Raja Chhatrapati Singh (1919–1998, Jhansi) — inspired by Swami Ramdas (a Kudau Singh disciple); composed chaturang/vedang/taalsagar pieces using 4/6/7/108-maatra calculations.
17: 1. Tripushkar (Natya Shastra) — a 3-part instrument inspired by raindrops on lotus leaves: Urdhwak (kept upright on the floor), Aalingya (strapped around the neck), Ankik (kept in the lap, 'ank' = thigh) — Aalingya faded for being awkward to hold; what remained became tabla. 2. Bhoomi-Dundubhi (Vedic) — hide stretched over a dug earthen pit, struck with sticks/danced on; a candidate root for ALL Indian percussion, tabla included. 3. Lala Bhawanidas Pakhawaaji — lost a pakhawaaj dangal (competition), smashed the instrument in anger, then guiltily glued it back; the resulting two pieces sounded different and became tabla and dagga ('toda tab bhi bola' — 'it spoke even after breaking' — hence 'tabla'). 4. Middle East — Sumerian/Babylonian 'balag' and terms like tabal baladi/turkey/jang/sami/mirgi (war-drums carried on camels) show a plausible name-lineage into 'tabla.'

5. Amir Khusro (12th c.) — credited by some with inventing tabla and devising taals/raags, but Madanul Mousiqi (Muhammad Qaram Imam) credits him only with 17 Persian-influenced taal/thekas, not tabla itself; Akbar-era Aaina-e-Akbari (16th c.) doesn't mention tabla at all, suggesting it postdates that period — also supported by the shahi's relatively advanced (and recent) construction. 6. Emperor Muhammad Shah II — employed Rehmat Khan (pakhawaaj) at court; his court also had a second Amir Khusro who studied khayal gayaki under Sadarang-Adarang. 7. Khayal gayaki's need — 17th c. khayal needed a lighter, more delicate percussion partner than pakhawaaj's heavy dhrupad-suited bass, prompting tabla's creation as a better match. 8. Khushro Khan — another candidate pakhawaaji of the same era; the name's similarity to 'Amir Khusro' may be why credit gets conflated between the two.

Shahi evolved from an iron-powder/starch/glue paste to a manganese-ore-based paste (river stones from Ahmedabad), built in dried, friction-smoothed layers. Dr. C.V. Raman scientifically analysed tabla's overtones/nodes and found shahi-bearing instruments produce ~20% more resonance/sustenance than those without (he also experimented unsuccessfully with monkey-skin and screw-tuning). Modern changes: clay dagga → copper/steel; animal-hide waadi → synthetic options in some instruments; double-pudi tablas tunable across 3–4 notes via nuts/bolts.

Tripushkar's Urdhwak evolved into 'Dardar', its Ankik into 'Panava' — both attested since ~5th c. BCE. Dardar → 'Dhari', linking to the Dharis proposed as the original tabla-playing community who later moved to Delhi and founded the Delhi gharana (whose founder, Ut. Siddhar Khan, carries the surname Dhari/Dhadi). Supporting evidence cited: cave/temple carvings of tabla-like instruments from as early as ~1 AD (e.g. Ajanta). Source: Umesh Moghe, 'The Origin and Expansion Disciplines of Delhi Tabla, Part 1.'
आज तबला का स्थान · Status, importance, application today

Versatility — equally at home in solo, kathak accompaniment, sitar/qawwali accompaniment, and (via thekas like bhikmaang) Bollywood. Accompaniment role — sometimes described as 'zameen banana' (making the ground/floor) for the main artist to build on. Internationalisation — Ut. Zakir Hussain's global concerts and fusion work (e.g. ensembles at Berklee) paralleling other Indian-classical internationalisation (Ut. Amjad Ali Khan at the 2014 Nobel concert, Pt. Ravi Shankar/Anoushka Shankar abroad). Popularisation of solos — a historical shift from royal-court (darbaar) presentation to public concert presentation across the 20th century, with figures like Ut. Ahmedjaan Thirakwa central to that transition.
18: Main artist chooses raag, taal, laya. Tabla must be precisely tuned to match. Laya stays undisturbed for the main performer unless they signal a change. Compositions should be neither bland nor excessive; what/where/how much to play differs by style and artist. Tabla shouldn't disturb the main composition's line of thought, and should fit the raag's time/mood. Accompaniment 'shouldn't be like a collage.' A strong accompanist needs imagination, observation, frequent listening, and a willingness to set ego aside — Ut. Alla Rakha and Ut. Habibuddin Khan are cited as exemplars.

Vilambit laya — the larger maatra-gap means the theka must be unmistakably clear so the singer can stay anchored in it. Fill the pauses (between maatras) with meaningful-but-unobtrusive bols (trake, ge, TRKT, dhagetrake) if the singer's resonance/aas needs support — never let the theka feel hollow, but never overload it either. Begin with a small mukhda before sum once the asthayi starts, then settle into theka.

Drut/madhya laya — small tihais before sum or extra bols between maatras are appropriate; signalled improvisation opportunities can use a flexible phrase like 'dhatidhagetinakena'; avoid 'tite' (kayda-coded). End improvised pieces with a short tihai, then resume theka.

Thumri/ghazal/naatya-sangeet use 'fickle'-natured taals matching the singing's fickle character — deepchandi, addha, keherwa, teentaal. Deepchandi commonly converts to keherwa once the laya doubles, opening room for laggi/ladi at single/double/quadruple speed. Bhajan uses dhumali; qawwali/dadra-type forms use dadra; laggi typically follows the first stanza, closing on a short tihai/tod. Taraana (drut laya) invites prominent tihais/tukdas — a chance to show riyaaz.

After the instrumentalist opens their gat: a wazandaar (weighty) avartan of theka, a couple avartans of uthaan, then continue theka — matching an avartan to whatever gat is played, using kayda bols as appropriate. A jhala gets a matching rela. When the main artist reaches drut laya, a small tihai bridges into continued drut theka; few new variations are needed there, but kissm (theka variation) keeps it interesting. Never speed up/slow down during the main artist's own tihai. Considered advanced accompaniment because instrumental phrasing/taal choices (even unconventional ones, e.g. 9.5 maatras) can diverge sharply from typical vocal patterns — live rehearsal with the instrumentalist matters.
वाद्य संगति — गायकी अंग व तंत अंग

Instrumental presentation moves through alaap → jod → masidkhani gat (vilambit, gayaki-ang/khayal-mirroring) → razakhani gat (drut, tant-ang) → jhala. Masidkhani gat is typically played in teentaal, jhaptaal, roopak, ektaal, ada-chautaal (occasionally matta, rudra). During the gat, peshkaar-style entry into a sum-landing tihai followed by a weighty theka is common; advanced layakaris (7-in-5, 10-in-7, 14-in-10, 8-in-9) may be called for. Jhala (mainly teentaal, sometimes ektaal) tests stamina — 'na dhin dhin na' and anudrut teentaal/ektaal practice pays off here.

Kathak accompaniment isn't as spontaneous as vocal/instrumental — every dancer has fixed gats, todas, chakradaars (varying by gharana) that need pre-rehearsal. The dance baaj leans khula baaj with gat-tode and chakradaars. Different rasas (shringar, karuna, shanta, gambhir) need matching tabla character. A strong soloist often makes a strong dance accompanist too.
सोलो और संगति का संबंध · Correlation with solo

A good soloist usually has the raw skill to become a good accompanist; the reverse isn't guaranteed — someone who only knows local thekas (e.g. bhikmaang, jaggu) won't accompany instruments/dance well. Deep riyaaz and broad study make a player flexible enough to accompany almost anything (even film songs). The accompanist should stay devoted to all styles even without being an expert performer of them, contributing to — rather than competing with — the main artist's success, while staying humble about prior solo reputation.
20: A solo opens with a salutation (to Goddess Saraswati, the instrument, the art form, the guru) before playing. Order moves vilambit → drut, paralleling singing: uthaan/peshkaar → kayda → rela → gat → tukda → chakradhaar → farmaishi chakradhaar → kamaali chakradhaar → paran → tihai (order can flex by gharana/baaj). Compositions move from most-expandable/improvisable (peshkaar — new bols allowed) to least (kayda/rela — no new bols) to fixed (drut-laya pieces, valued for the tayyari needed to memorise them) — most improvisation happens in the first half, letting the player's thinking mature as the solo progresses. The performance closes with thanks to the audience.

Begin with a respectful greeting and stable seating/posture; finish within the organiser's time limit. Daily practice at a fixed time, balancing strength and nazaakat (delicacy), builds the in-depth laya/composition knowledge a solo needs. A soloist should be able to recite (padhant) the bandishes they play, stay reader of audience mood, and show command of gharana/baaj/nikaas — eventually even absorbing the thinking-styles of other scholars. Tuning awareness matters throughout. Playing loud isn't the same as playing powerfully — an all-rounded presentation matters more than volume. Most solos are in teentaal, but also jhaptaal/pancham sawari/roopak/matta; the lehra/nagma must complement the taal's vibhaag. A player moving into an accompanist role mid-performance should stay alert to the main artist.

Vocal recitation of a composition — taught from the very start of tabla education (with taali/khaali shown by hand) and used throughout tabla, pakhawaaj, and kathak performance. Convention: name the composer respectfully, then recite the composition. Practising padhant slow-to-fast builds the ability to pronounce fast compositions cleanly and impressively in performance. Personal benefits go beyond memorisation: repeating a composition vocally reveals its vazan (weight) and hidden structural nuance, eventually translating into more expressive hands and greater performance confidence. In concert, spoken padhant (with a short verbal description) also helps the audience follow what a fixed composition is and enjoy it more.
रियाज़ व दायाँ-बायाँ संतुलन · Riyaaz & hand balance

A good solo shows balance between daya (tabla) and baya (dagga) expression, not just dexterity on one side. Riyaaz routines vary by artist — Ut. Ahmedjaan Thirakwa's reported 14–15 hours/day is the most-cited example. Within kayda riyaaz, the practice-categories murakka and chilla are themselves examined — see this card's own flag box for the safe exam phrasing on that distinction, since it's one of the project's open guru-confirmation items.
